facts.statement: Nannopterygius is an extinct genus of ophthalmosaurid ichthyosaur whose name means "small wing/flipper" in Greek.
facts.quote: Nannopterygius (meaning "small wing/flipper" in Greek) is an extinct genus of ophthalmosaurid ichthyosaur that lived during the Middle Jurassic to the Early Cretaceous (Callovian to Berriasian stages).

facts.statement: Nannopterygius was a small ichthyosaur that reached a maximum length of 3.5 meters.
facts.quote: Nannopterygius was small for an ichthyosaur, measuring up to 3.5 m long at maximum.

facts.statement: The head of Nannopterygius was 50 centimeters long and featured a long, narrow snout.
facts.quote: The head is 50 cm long, with a typical long narrow rostrum.

facts.statement: Nannopterygius had large eyes with a bony scleral ring, a feature characteristic of ophthalmosaurids.
facts.quote: The eyes are large, hence its classification as an ophthalmosaurid, and have a bony scleral ring inside the eye socket.

facts.statement: Nannopterygius possessed at least 60 disc-shaped vertebrae, indicating it was flexible, agile, and likely a fast swimmer.
facts.quote: There are at least 60 disc-shaped vertebrae, although owing to the condition of the fossil it is not possible to tell exactly how many there were, showing that Nannopterygius was flexible, agile and probably a fast swimmer.

facts.statement: Unlike its relative Ophthalmosaurus, Nannopterygius had much smaller paddles, measuring 25-30 cm for the forepaddles and only 10-15 cm for the hindpaddles.
facts.quote: Most of the features are very similar to the close relative Ophthalmosaurus. However, its paddles are much smaller, around 25-30 cm for the forepaddles and only 10-15 cm for the hindpaddles.

facts.statement: Nannopterygius had a streamlined, torpedo-shaped body that made it an inefficient long-distance swimmer but capable of speed over short distances.
facts.quote: This gave it a very streamlined, torpedo-shaped look, but would have made it quite difficult to generate much lift or to turn quickly, making it an inefficient long-distance swimmer but speedy over short distances.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Nannopterygius may have been an ambush predator that quickly plunged into shoals of fish in shallow seas.
facts.quote: It is therefore possible that it was an ambush predator which plunged into shoals of fish quickly in the shallow seas where it lived.

facts.statement: The first specimen of Nannopterygius was found in the Kimmeridge Clay Formation of Dorset, UK, and described by Hulke in 1871 as Ichthyosaurus enthekiodon.
facts.quote: The first specimen was found in the Kimmeridgian Kimmeridge Clay Formation of Kimmeridge Bay, Dorset, UK and described by Hulke in 1871, who named it Ichthyosaurus enthekiodon.

facts.statement: Friedrich von Huene established the genus Nannopterygius in 1922, naming it after the animal's small paddles.
facts.quote: In 1922, Friedrich von Huene separated this species into the new genus Nannopterygius, named for the small fore- and hindpaddles.

facts.statement: In 2020, several new species of Nannopterygius were named based on fossils found in Norway and Russia.
facts.quote: In 2020, several more species, including N. borealis, and the species once contained in the genera Paraophthalmosaurus and Yasykovia were named based on remains found in Norway and Russia.

facts.statement: Two additional species of Nannopterygius from Kazakhstan were confirmed in 2022.
facts.quote: The existence of two more species from Kazakhstan, N. mikhailovi and N. yakimenkae, was confirmed by Yakupova & Akhmedenov (2022).

facts.statement: Fossils of Nannopterygius have been found in England, Kazakhstan, Russia, and Norway.
facts.quote: Fossils are known from England, Kazakhstan, Russia, and Norway and six species are currently assigned to the genus.

facts.statement: During the Late Jurassic, Europe was an island archipelago surrounded by warm, tropical seas.
facts.quote: At the time, Europe represented an island archipelago which was closer to the equator than it is today, surrounded by warm, tropical seas.

facts.statement: The Kimmeridge Clay Formation represents an offshore marine environment where the seafloor was deep enough to avoid storm disturbance.
facts.quote: The Kimmeridge Clay specifically represents an offshore marine environment, in which the seafloor was far enough below the surface not to be disturbed by storms.

facts.statement: The species N. yasykovi and N. saveljeviensis are found in the Volga region of Russia, which defines the Volgian stage.
facts.quote: The species N. yasykovi and N. saveljeviensis are known from the Volga region of Russia, which gives the Volgian stage its name.

facts.statement: The species N. borealis is known from earliest Cretaceous sediments in the Slottsmøya Member of the Agardhfjellet Formation.
facts.quote: Additionally, the species N. borealis is known from earliest Cretaceous sediments of the Slottsmøya Member of the Agardhfjellet Formation.

facts.statement: The seafloor at the Slottsmøya site was located about 150 meters below the surface and was relatively oxygen-poor.
facts.quote: The seafloor, which was located about 150 m below the surface, seems to have been relatively dysoxic, or oxygen-poor, although it was periodically oxygenated by clastic sediments.

facts.statement: The Slottsmøya Member contains fossils of other marine reptiles such as Undorosaurus, Arthropterygius, and Brachypterygius alongside Nannopterygius.
facts.quote: In addition to Nannopterygius, the Slottsmøya Member presents a diverse assemblage of other marine reptiles, including the ichthyosaurs Undorosaurus gorodischensis, several species belonging to the genus Arthropterygius, and a partial skull attributed to Brachypterygius sp.

facts.statement: An analysis by Zverkov and Jacobs (2020) identified Nannopterygius as the sister taxon to Thalassodraco within Ophthalmosauria.
facts.quote: The following cladogram shows a possible phylogenetic position of Nannopterygius, which was found to be the sister taxon to Thalassodraco, in Ophthalmosauria according to an analysis performed by Zverkov and Jacobs (2020).

facts.statement: Nannopterygius belongs to the family Ophthalmosauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Ophthalmosauridae

facts.statement: Nannopterygius is a genus of ophthalmosaurid ichthyosaur that lived during the Late Jurassic periods of Kimmeridgian and Tithonian.
facts.quote: Nannopterygius (que significa "pequeña aleta") es un género de ictiosaurio oftalmosáurido que vivió en el Jurásico tardío (periodos Kimmeridgiense y Titoniense).

facts.statement: Nannopterygius lived from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian stages, between 154.8 and 143.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Kimmeridgian to Tithonian (154.8 to 143.1 million years ago)
